Daily internet users - professionals and younger adults who rely on the internet for work and personal communication, using it every day across multiple devices.
Regular but not daily users - middle-aged adults who use the internet most days for news, email, and social purposes but maintain some offline time.
Moderate users - people who access the internet a few times a week for specific needs like banking, shopping, or information gathering but don't depend on it constantly.
Occasional users - older adults or those with limited digital engagement who use the internet only occasionally for essential tasks, preferring traditional methods.
Non-users - elderly or digitally disconnected individuals who rarely or never use the internet, representing a small but persistent segment resistant to digital adoption.

Progressive cohabiters who have lived with partners without marriage and strongly approve of this lifestyle choice. They view cohabitation as a normal, acceptable alternative to marriage and likely support LGBTQ+ rights as well.

Pragmatic acceptors who have cohabited or are open to it, viewing it as a practical arrangement. They neither strongly approve nor disapprove, seeing cohabitation as a personal choice without moral judgment.

Traditional married individuals who have not cohabited before marriage and maintain conventional views about relationships. They may disapprove of cohabitation but are a minority in this relatively liberal Dutch group.

Neutral observers without strong personal experience or conviction about cohabitation. They sit in the middle ground, neither approving nor disapproving, reflecting the significant portion of the group that remains undecided on lifestyle choices.

Strict traditionalists who disapprove of cohabitation and view marriage as the only appropriate framework for partnership. This is a small minority in the Netherlands, even among those with lower secondary education.

Engaged civic participants - typically better educated, regularly online, religiously affiliated, and actively involved in community organizations. They see organizational work as a natural part of civic responsibility.

Passive citizens - moderate internet users who are religiously engaged but lack strong motivation for organizational involvement. They support community work in principle but don't actively participate.

Economically stressed non-participants - struggling with household finances and focused on daily survival rather than voluntary association work. They have limited time and energy for organizational involvement.

Digital-first individualists - heavy daily internet users, often secular, who prefer informal online engagement over traditional organizational structures. They may volunteer but through non-traditional channels.
Disconnected outsiders - occasional or non-internet users, often older or from rural areas, with limited exposure to organizational opportunities. They rarely engage in formal association work.
Politically engaged centrists and moderate left-leaning voters who feel a genuine connection to a mainstream party that aligns with their progressive but pragmatic values on social issues.
Socially liberal but politically detached citizens who approve of modern lifestyles yet feel disconnected from all political parties and prefer to remain independent.
Right-leaning or conservative voters with stronger religious affiliation who identify with parties defending traditional values, though they represent a smaller minority in this age group.
Left-wing activists and union members who feel closest to left-wing or far-left parties that champion workers' rights and progressive social policies.
Disillusioned or apathetic citizens who reject traditional party politics entirely, viewing all mainstream parties as inadequate despite their socially liberal views.

Progressive urbanites with strong LGBTQ+ acceptance. They would strongly disagree with feeling ashamed, viewing such feelings as discriminatory and contrary to modern values of equality and personal freedom.

Socially liberal but somewhat cautious individuals. They would disagree with feeling ashamed, though perhaps less emphatically, reflecting general acceptance while maintaining some traditional social perspectives.

Neutral or conflicted individuals, possibly from more traditional backgrounds or with limited exposure to LGBTQ+ issues. They neither agree nor disagree, uncertain about their own feelings on this personal matter.
Traditionally-minded individuals with conservative values. They would agree they might feel some shame, reflecting discomfort with homosexuality based on religious or traditional family beliefs.
Strongly conservative individuals with deep traditional or religious convictions. They would strongly agree with feeling ashamed, viewing homosexuality as fundamentally at odds with their values.
Digitally active retirees who remain engaged with learning and self-improvement. They regularly use the internet daily and see value in continuing education to stay current with modern skills.
Moderately engaged older adults who use the internet frequently but view their working years as behind them. They see little practical need for professional development courses at this stage of life.
Socially conservative retirees with limited internet use who prioritize traditional activities and family time over formal learning. They are unlikely to pursue structured educational courses.

Health-conscious, civically engaged retirees who maintain some internet presence and occasional interest in intellectual stimulation through lectures or conferences on topics of personal interest rather than work-related skills.
Digitally disconnected older adults who rarely use the internet and have minimal engagement with formal learning institutions. They see no relevance to work-related training at their life stage.
Progressive urbanites who embrace modern family structures and see cohabitation and non-traditional partnerships as acceptable lifestyle choices. They approve of having children outside marriage.

Pragmatic moderates who neither strongly approve nor disapprove of unmarried cohabitation and childbearing, viewing it as a personal choice without moral judgment. They represent the largest neutral middle ground.
Traditional conservatives who disapprove of having children outside marriage on moral or religious grounds, believing marriage should precede parenthood. They hold traditional family values.
Conflicted traditionalists who personally avoid cohabitation and unmarried childbearing but are becoming more accepting of others' choices, sitting between disapproval and neutrality.
Strong traditionalists who strongly disapprove of unmarried cohabitation and childbearing, viewing it as morally wrong and harmful to society and children.

Women from traditional Catholic families where mothers stayed home to raise children, reflecting the strong religious values (92% religious) and traditional gender roles common in Poland during the 1980s-90s.

Women whose mothers worked as employees in state enterprises or public sector jobs, the dominant employment model in communist and post-communist Poland, representing the most common maternal work pattern.
Women from rural or agricultural backgrounds whose mothers were self-employed farmers or engaged in agricultural work, reflecting Poland's significant rural population.
Women whose mothers had passed away or were absent during their childhood, a notable minority given Poland's historical circumstances and life expectancy patterns of that era.
Women from entrepreneurial or small business families where mothers were self-employed in non-agricultural sectors, representing the emerging private sector in 1990s Poland.
Daily digital workers: Professionals and office workers who rely on the internet constantly for their jobs and personal communication, using multiple devices throughout the day.
Regular internet users: People who use the internet most days for work-related tasks and some personal purposes, maintaining consistent but not constant online presence.
Moderate users: Those who access the internet a few times a week for specific needs like email, banking, or occasional browsing, but don't depend on it daily.
Occasional users: Older workers or those in less digitalized roles who use the internet only occasionally for necessary tasks, reflecting lower digital integration in their work.
Non-users: A small segment with minimal or no internet use, either due to age, job type, or limited digital skills and access.
Working-class individuals with stable employment who have joined unions to protect their labor rights and secure better working conditions; they see union membership as a practical necessity.
Former union members from earlier career stages who have since left the workforce, retired, or changed to non-unionized work; they maintain some connection to organized labor from their past.
Self-employed workers, small business owners, and informal sector workers who have never had access to or need for union membership; they view unions as irrelevant to their work situation.

Young workers and precarious employees in gig or temporary positions who lack stable employment and have not joined unions despite potential benefits; they see unions as disconnected from their reality.
Individuals in non-unionized private sector jobs who have consciously avoided union involvement, either due to employer opposition or personal preference for individual negotiation.

Pragmatic centrists who are financially stable and socially moderate. They feel reasonably connected to mainstream political institutions and see value in having a preferred party that represents their interests, even if imperfectly.

Disengaged skeptics struggling financially who feel alienated from the political system. They don't feel close to any party because they believe none adequately represent working people or address their economic concerns.
Religiously-oriented conservatives with traditional values who have a clear political home. They identify strongly with a party that aligns with their religious beliefs and social conservatism.

Socially liberal, educated professionals who are economically comfortable but politically independent. They may sympathize with certain parties on specific issues but resist strong partisan identification.
Union-affiliated workers with established political loyalties. They feel connected to a party through their labor organization ties and see it as defending their class interests.
Rural agricultural workers and small farmers with traditional employment patterns who have never had formal union membership, viewing unions as irrelevant to their self-employed or family-based work.
Older workers who were union members during their working years in manufacturing or public sector roles but have since retired, maintaining a positive view of unions from their past experience.

Younger, less politically engaged villagers with limited exposure to union culture who have never considered joining and see unions as something for industrial workers in cities, not rural communities.
Small business owners and self-employed artisans who actively reject union membership as incompatible with their independent economic status and village-based livelihoods.
A small minority of current or recent union members, likely in public sector or larger local employers, who maintain active membership as part of their professional identity.
Progressive urbanites with liberal values who approve of cohabitation and have likely lived with partners themselves. They see cohabitation as a normal, acceptable lifestyle choice.
Pragmatic moderates who are neutral or mildly approving of cohabitation as a practical arrangement. They may or may not have personal experience with it, but don't see it as problematic.
Traditional-leaning individuals who disapprove of cohabitation on moral or religious grounds and have not lived with unmarried partners. They view marriage as the proper framework for shared living.

Socially conservative union members or working-class Finns who hold traditional values but recognize cohabitation as increasingly common. They may disapprove personally while acknowledging its prevalence.
Younger or more secular Finns who are indifferent to the cohabitation question, neither strongly approving nor disapproving. They view it as a personal choice without moral significance.
Pragmatic mainstream workers who trust Swiss institutions and regulatory processes. They view vaccination as a straightforward public health measure and are likely to get vaccinated or already have.

Cautious but compliant individuals who have some hesitations about rapid vaccine development but ultimately defer to national regulatory authority approval. They will likely get vaccinated eventually, though perhaps with some delay.
Skeptical citizens with concerns about pharmaceutical companies, government mandates, or medical autonomy. They are unlikely to get vaccinated regardless of regulatory approval.
Health-conscious individuals focused on natural immunity or alternative approaches who question the necessity of vaccination. They tend toward vaccine hesitancy despite regulatory approval.
Ideologically-driven vaccine opponents who distrust authorities and regulatory bodies on principle. They actively reject vaccination and may view it as a violation of personal freedom.

Engaged professionals and lifelong learners who regularly use the internet daily and actively participate in organizations; they view continuous professional development as essential and regularly take courses or attend conferences to stay competitive.

Moderately active workers with consistent internet use who recognize the value of skill development; they take courses or attend conferences occasionally when they feel it's necessary for their career progression.

Pragmatic individuals with moderate internet engagement who take a selective approach to professional development; they only pursue training when directly required by their employer or when facing specific skill gaps.

Less digitally engaged older workers with limited internet use who see little need for formal professional development at this stage of their careers; they rely on existing experience and rarely attend courses or conferences.
Disengaged individuals with minimal organizational participation and low internet usage who actively avoid or show no interest in professional development activities.
Healthy individuals with minimal healthcare needs who rarely require medical treatment and thus haven't experienced waiting list issues.
People with occasional healthcare needs who have accessed treatment without significant delays, viewing the Australian system as generally functional despite some wait times.
Individuals with chronic or ongoing conditions who have experienced frustrating delays in accessing needed medical treatment due to long waiting lists.
People with serious health concerns who have managed to access timely treatment through private healthcare or by navigating the public system effectively, avoiding major delays.
Those with complex medical needs who have experienced significant barriers to treatment access and view waiting lists as a serious problem in Australian healthcare.
Devout believers who accept religious miracles as real manifestations of divine power and see them as evidence of God's active presence in the world.
Moderate believers who think miracles probably occur but maintain some skepticism, viewing them as possible but not certain or requiring strong evidence.
Uncertain pragmatists who are genuinely undecided about miracles, often due to limited personal experience or conflicting cultural and modern influences in village life.
Skeptical doubters who probably don't believe in religious miracles, attributing unusual events to natural causes or coincidence rather than divine intervention.
Firm disbelievers who definitively reject the concept of miracles as incompatible with their understanding of how the world works.

Religious followers with traditional beliefs who see their faith as treating men and women according to complementary roles, with men in leadership positions; they select 'Treats men better than women' or 'Treats men and women equally' depending on how they rationalize traditional structures.

Religious practitioners, particularly those following Christianity or Islam (dominant in Suriname), who genuinely believe their religion teaches equality between genders despite acknowledging some traditional practices; they choose 'Treats men and women equally.'

Non-religious or secular individuals who recognize gender inequality in religious institutions and explicitly reject religious frameworks; they select 'I don't belong to or follow any religion' as their answer.
Spiritual but non-religious people who are critical of organized religion's gender practices and see religions as treating men better; they choose 'Treats men better than women.'
Uncertain respondents across various belief categories who struggle to assess gender equality in religious contexts or are uncomfortable making judgments; they select 'Can't choose.'
Secular materialists who reject religious concepts entirely. They see life after death as scientifically implausible and definitely do not believe in it.
Skeptical agnostics uncertain about metaphysical claims. They probably do not believe in life after death but remain open to the possibility they could be wrong.

Spiritual but non-religious people who believe in some form of higher power or transcendence. They probably believe in some form of life after death, though not necessarily in traditional religious terms.
Culturally religious or doubtful believers who maintain some faith despite reservations. They probably believe in life after death as part of their residual religious worldview.
Committed religious believers with strong conviction in God and the afterlife. They definitely believe in life after death as a core part of their faith.

Working-class residents with modest incomes who see themselves as solidly middle or lower-middle on the social ladder, neither privileged nor at the very bottom, reflecting their stable but constrained economic position in small-town Russia.
Lower-income individuals who perceive themselves in the bottom half of society, having experienced economic pressures and limited opportunities typical of struggling small-town communities.

Relatively better-off locals—small business owners, professionals, or those with stable government jobs—who place themselves in the upper-middle range, viewing themselves as more successful than average in their community.

Skeptical or disengaged respondents uncertain about social hierarchy itself, who struggle to position themselves and may view the question as reflecting Soviet-era thinking or as irrelevant to their actual circumstances.
Aspirational individuals who rate themselves higher than their objective circumstances might suggest, reflecting optimism or a desire to distance themselves from lower social positions.
Secular materialists who reject both religion and spirituality as meaningful frameworks for understanding life and meaning.
Spiritual seekers without institutional religion who find meaning in personal spiritual exploration, often drawing from Buddhist or Taoist traditions without formal practice.
Religious practitioners who follow Buddhism or folk religion as part of their cultural identity and maintain both religious practice and spiritual beliefs.
Casual believers who maintain some religious affiliation (often Buddhism) but don't consider themselves particularly spiritual or actively engaged in practice.
Undecided individuals who are uncertain about their relationship to religion and spirituality and prefer not to commit to a clear position.
Secular skeptics who reject religious concepts entirely. They don't believe in miracles and see them as superstition or misinterpretation of natural events.
Pragmatic agnostics uncertain about miracles. They can't decide whether miracles are real and remain genuinely undecided on the question.
Cautious believers who think miracles might exist but aren't confident. They lean toward belief but acknowledge significant doubt.
Committed believers in religious miracles. They have faith that miracles do occur and see them as evidence of spiritual reality.
Doubtful skeptics who lean against miracles but leave some room for possibility. They think miracles probably don't happen but aren't absolutely certain.
Environmentally committed activists who regularly recycle and take direct action on environmental issues, viewing petition-signing as a natural extension of their conservation values.
Moderately engaged environmentalists who recycle often and care about sustainability, but are selective about which environmental causes they actively support through petitions.
Casual recyclers with general environmental concern who haven't signed environmental petitions, either due to lack of awareness of specific campaigns or limited motivation to take that step.
Skeptical or disengaged individuals who recycle minimally and view environmental petitions as ineffective or not worth their time.
Ideologically driven non-participants who may recycle but oppose environmental activism on principle, viewing petition campaigns as alarmist or politically motivated.
Religious traditionalists with strong Catholic faith who believe same-sex relations are morally wrong based on church teachings and traditional values.
Moderately religious people who have some moral reservations about same-sex relations but are not absolutist, seeing it as wrong only in certain contexts or holding nuanced views.
Secular or non-religious individuals who see no moral problem with consensual same-sex relations between adults and view it as a personal choice.
Conflicted believers who hold religious faith but struggle with traditional teachings on sexuality, leaning toward acceptance while experiencing some internal doubt.
Undecided or uncertain people who lack a clear moral framework on this issue and prefer not to make a definitive judgment.

Standard public insurance holders: Married Germans with stable employment who rely on the national public health insurance system (option H), viewing it as the standard and sufficient coverage for their needs.

Supplementary coverage seekers: Married individuals with public insurance who have added private complementary insurance (option E) to cover gaps and access additional services beyond basic public coverage.

Employer-based insurance users: Married professionals whose health insurance is primarily provided through their employer or union (option F), representing a smaller but established segment of the workforce.

Private insurance holders: Married Germans with higher incomes or self-employed status who have opted for private insurance (option G) as their primary coverage, seeking more choice and personalized care.

Multi-coverage combination users: Married individuals with complex insurance arrangements combining multiple types such as employer-based plus private plus public coverage (option B), typically higher earners managing layered protection.
Committed atheists who reject religious belief entirely. They strongly disagree that God concerns himself with individuals, viewing this as a comforting but unfounded claim.

Secular pragmatists who are non-believers but not strongly opposed to religion. They tend to disagree with the statement, seeing no evidence for personal divine concern, though they're not hostile to those who believe.
Agnostics and the genuinely uncertain who neither fully accept nor reject the idea of a personal God. They sit in the middle, unsure whether God exists or intervenes in individual lives.
Moderate believers who accept God's existence and believe in some form of divine care, though perhaps not in a highly personal or interventionist way. They tend to agree with the statement.

Committed theists with strong personal faith who firmly believe God is actively concerned with each individual's life. They strongly agree with the statement based on their lived religious conviction.

Secular non-believers who have abandoned childhood Catholic faith and see themselves as neither religious nor spiritual, representing a significant portion of French Catholics who have become atheist or agnostic.
Cultural Catholics who maintain nominal religious identity but don't actively practice or believe in core doctrines like hell, viewing themselves as spiritual but not religiously observant.
Practicing believers who follow Catholicism as both a religion and spiritual practice, regularly engaging with scripture and maintaining traditional Catholic beliefs.
Spiritual seekers without institutional religion who have rejected organized Catholicism but retain some spiritual sensibility and may occasionally engage with religious texts.
Conflicted middle-ground individuals who follow religion nominally but lack strong spiritual conviction, uncertain about their relationship to faith and unable to clearly categorize themselves.
Secular skeptics who reject religious concepts entirely. They see hell as a mythological construct with no basis in reality and are confident in their disbelief.
Agnostic doubters uncertain about religious matters. They acknowledge hell might exist but have significant doubts, reflecting their general ambivalence toward religious doctrine.
Moderate believers who accept traditional Christian teachings including hell, though without absolute certainty. They see hell as probably real within a framework of Christian belief.
Committed religious believers who are confident in hell's existence as part of their faith. They view hell as a definite spiritual reality central to their worldview.
Undecided individuals genuinely unable to form a position on hell. They may lack religious background, find the question unanswerable, or simply haven't considered it seriously.
Secular materialists who find meaning through relationships, work, and personal achievement rather than religion. They strongly disagree that life's meaning depends on God.
Agnostic pragmatists who are uncertain about God's existence and remain neutral on whether divine meaning is necessary. They see life as potentially meaningful regardless of religious belief.
Moderate believers who accept God's existence but don't see it as the sole source of life's meaning. They find purpose through multiple sources including faith, family, and personal goals.
Committed religious individuals for whom God is central to their worldview and the primary foundation of life's meaning. They strongly agree that existence without God would be meaningless.
Undecided individuals who haven't formed a clear position on the relationship between God and life's meaning. They struggle to choose between religious and secular frameworks.
Religious traditionalists with strong faith convictions who regularly engage with scripture as part of their spiritual practice and daily religious observance.
Moderately religious individuals who believe in God with some doubts but occasionally read or listen to scripture, viewing it as culturally and spiritually important.
Secular or non-religious Israelis who rarely or never read scripture, either due to lack of belief in God or viewing religious texts as irrelevant to their lives.
Culturally Jewish Israelis who maintain some connection to Torah and Jewish texts for cultural or historical reasons rather than deep religious conviction.
Uncertain or ambivalent individuals who sometimes believe in God and may occasionally encounter scripture but lack consistent engagement with religious texts.
Secular materialists: Non-religious and explicitly reject spirituality as meaningful. They view the world through a rational, scientific lens and see no value in spiritual frameworks.
Spiritual seekers: Don't follow organized religion but maintain personal spiritual beliefs and practices. They find meaning in spirituality without institutional religious structures.
Cultural Christians: Follow Christianity nominally, often for cultural or traditional reasons rather than deep conviction. They may not be particularly spiritual but maintain religious identity.
Committed believers: Follow a religion and consider themselves genuinely spiritual people. They integrate faith and spirituality into their worldview and daily life.
Ambivalent agnostics: Uncertain about religion and spirituality, neither clearly rejecting nor embracing either. They remain open to spiritual ideas but don't commit to religious practice.
Progressive secularists who reject traditional gender roles entirely. They strongly disagree with the statement, viewing it as outdated and incompatible with modern equality.
Moderate egalitarians who believe in gender equality but may acknowledge some traditional perspectives exist. They disagree with the statement but without strong conviction.
Pragmatic middle-grounders uncertain about gender roles in practice. They neither fully agree nor disagree, seeing merit in both traditional and modern arrangements.
Conservative traditionalists who believe in complementary gender roles with some modern flexibility. They agree with the statement's basic premise but may not strongly emphasize it.
Religious traditionalists who strongly support traditional gender divisions based on religious conviction. They strongly agree with the statement as reflecting proper family structure.
Committed Catholics who accept core doctrines including hell as part of traditional faith teaching, viewing it as a real spiritual reality.
Moderate believers who acknowledge hell probably exists as Catholic doctrine teaches it, but without strong conviction or deep concern about it.
Skeptical Catholics who doubt hell's existence or reject it as incompatible with a merciful God, leaning toward disbelief.
Secular or lapsed Catholics who definitively reject hell as a medieval concept with no basis in reality.
Uncertain individuals who cannot decide on hell's existence due to conflicting doubts about religious teachings or lack of conviction.
Environmentally engaged activists who regularly sign petitions and take action on environmental issues as part of their civic participation.
Moderately concerned citizens who care about environmental issues and have signed a petition occasionally when they encountered one that resonated with them.
Skeptical pragmatists who doubt the effectiveness of petitions and prefer other forms of environmental engagement or see them as performative.
Disengaged individuals who have not signed environmental petitions due to lack of awareness, low prioritization, or general apathy toward activism.
Uncertain fence-sitters who are sympathetic to environmental concerns but haven't clearly committed to petition-signing as a form of action.
Environmentally conscious recyclers who make recycling a regular habit and see it as a personal responsibility, reflecting the group's generally progressive values on social issues.
Pragmatic occasional recyclers who sort materials sometimes when convenient, balancing environmental concern with the realities of daily life in urban Taiwan.
Indifferent non-recyclers who rarely or never make special effort to sort recyclables, either due to lack of awareness or prioritizing convenience over environmental impact.
Systematic recyclers who always participate in sorting because they view it as a civic duty and part of maintaining social order, consistent with the group's moderate-to-progressive leanings.
Skeptical minimalists who question the effectiveness of individual recycling efforts and see it as performative, reflecting some diversity of opinion within the otherwise consensus-oriented group.

Economically struggling individuals who have experienced significant hardship due to Venezuela's economic crisis and see themselves at the bottom of the social hierarchy with little hope of upward mobility.
Lower-middle class workers who maintain some economic stability but feel vulnerable and perceive themselves in the lower-to-middle range of society, uncertain about their position.
Young professionals or skilled workers who have managed to secure relatively better employment and view themselves as solidly middle class, placing themselves in the middle range of the scale.
Individuals with higher education or professional credentials who believe they occupy upper-middle positions in society despite economic challenges, positioning themselves in the upper-middle range.
Those who are uncertain or refuse to make clear judgments about their social position, either due to the instability of Venezuelan society or philosophical reluctance to rank themselves.
Secular atheists from non-religious backgrounds. They don't believe in God, reject religious frameworks entirely, and see no value in spirituality or religious practice.

Non-religious but spiritually inclined individuals. They've moved away from organized religion but maintain personal spiritual beliefs and practices, finding meaning outside traditional religious structures.

Cultural or nominal religious followers. They were raised in a faith tradition (likely Christian given Germany's demographics) and maintain some religious identity, but don't actively practice or deeply believe in core doctrines like hell.
Committed religious believers who actively follow their faith. They believe in God, maintain religious practice, and accept traditional religious teachings as part of their worldview.
Undecided or ambivalent individuals. They struggle to categorize themselves clearly regarding religion and spirituality, uncertain about their beliefs and commitments.
Secular skeptics who reject religious claims entirely. They see miracles as scientifically implausible and view miracle claims as superstition or misinterpretation of natural events.
Moderate non-believers who are open-minded but unconvinced. They probably don't believe in miracles but acknowledge uncertainty and don't dismiss the possibility outright.

Uncertain agnostics who genuinely cannot decide on the question. They may have cultural Catholic background but lack strong conviction either way, reflecting the high 'can't choose' responses seen in some previous questions.
Cautious believers who probably accept that miracles could occur within a religious framework. They lean toward belief but aren't dogmatic, reflecting moderate faith without absolute certainty.
Committed religious believers who definitely believe in miracles as expressions of divine intervention. They view miracles as real spiritual phenomena consistent with their faith.
Religious traditionalists with strong faith conviction who regularly engage with Jewish texts and scripture as part of their observant lifestyle and spiritual practice.
Believers with moderate to strong faith who occasionally read or listen to Torah and other religious texts, but not as a consistent daily or weekly practice.
Secular or culturally Jewish individuals who rarely or never read religious scripture, viewing Judaism more as cultural identity than religious practice.
Doubtful or questioning believers who have some interest in understanding their faith tradition through scripture but engage with it sporadically and without strong conviction.
Non-believers or agnostics within the Jewish community who have little to no interest in reading religious texts regardless of their cultural background.
Pragmatic middle-class workers who see themselves as solidly average in society's hierarchy, neither struggling nor privileged, placing themselves around the middle of the scale (5-6).
Modest but satisfied employed professionals who feel they've achieved reasonable stability and position themselves slightly above the middle (7-8), reflecting some career success.
Working people with economic concerns who perceive themselves as below average in the social hierarchy, placing themselves in the lower-middle range (3-4), reflecting financial pressures.
Optimistic or successful individuals in paid work who view themselves as upper-middle or top tier (9-10), confident in their social and economic position.
Uncertain respondents who struggle to self-assess their position in society's hierarchy and may avoid committing to a specific placement.

Secular progressives with egalitarian values. They strongly reject traditional gender roles as outdated and incompatible with modern equality. They represent the largest secular contingent in Switzerland and view this statement as fundamentally contrary to contemporary values.

Religious traditionalists who follow established faith practices. They tend to agree with or feel neutral about traditional gender role divisions, seeing them as consistent with their religious teachings and cultural heritage.

Moderate pragmatists without strong religious conviction. They disagree with the statement but not vehemently, recognizing that while traditional roles exist in some families, they shouldn't be prescriptive or universal in modern society.

Undecided middle-ground individuals. They struggle to take a clear position, either because they see merit in both traditional stability and modern equality, or because they haven't formed strong opinions on gender roles.

Conservative believers in traditional family structures. They actively agree with the statement, viewing complementary gender roles as natural, beneficial for family stability, and aligned with their worldview.
Environmentally conscious recyclers who make recycling a regular habit and see it as a personal responsibility, reflecting the secular, progressive values common in this French group.
Occasional recyclers who sort materials sometimes when convenient, balancing environmental concerns with practical constraints of daily life.
Indifferent non-recyclers who rarely or never make special efforts to sort recyclables, either due to lack of motivation or skepticism about recycling's impact.

Conflicted middle-grounders who are uncertain about recycling practices and may feel ambivalent about whether their individual efforts matter, similar to the 'can't choose' tendency seen in religious questions.
Pragmatic recyclers who always recycle when infrastructure makes it easy and accessible, viewing it as a civic duty aligned with French environmental regulations rather than personal conviction.
Committed Christian believers who actively engage with their faith through regular scripture reading and prayer, viewing God as central to their life's meaning and identity.
Cultural or nominal Christians who believe in God and follow Christianity but with less intensity, often uncertain about doctrinal matters like hell and less frequent in personal religious practice.
Spiritual but non-religious seekers who reject organized religion but maintain some spiritual beliefs or practices, representing a bridge between faith and secularism.
Former believers who no longer hold religious faith after previously believing in God, often having moved away from Christianity but retaining some cultural or spiritual sensibilities.
Secular non-believers who reject both religion and spirituality entirely, viewing life as meaningful without God and seeing religious frameworks as unnecessary.
Secular skeptics who reject religious concepts outright. They see hell as a mythological construct with no basis in reality and are confident in their disbelief.
Agnostic doubters uncertain about supernatural claims. They lean toward skepticism about hell but acknowledge they cannot be certain, reflecting the Norwegian tendency toward religious ambivalence.
Moderate believers who accept some religious framework. They see hell as possibly real within a Christian worldview but are not strongly convinced of its existence.
Committed religious believers who accept traditional Christian doctrine. They believe hell is real as part of their faith, though they may not dwell on it constantly.
Genuinely undecided individuals who find the question unanswerable. They lack sufficient conviction in any direction and prefer to withhold judgment on metaphysical matters.
Committed believers who have always believed in God and remain confident in their faith, viewing God's existence as certain or nearly certain.
Wavering believers who currently believe in God but have doubts, representing those with faith that has evolved or fluctuated over time.
Secular non-believers who have never believed in God and remain atheist or agnostic, representing the substantial non-religious segment of the group.
Former believers who once had faith but no longer believe in God, having undergone a shift away from religious conviction.
Uncertain and undecided individuals who struggle to articulate their position on God and may identify as spiritual without clear theistic commitment.

State-dependent workers with public coverage: Employed individuals relying on Russia's mandatory public health insurance system (COMPULSORY MEDICAL INSURANCE - CMI), the standard for most employed Russians.
Dual-coverage pragmatists: Married professionals who maintain both public health insurance and supplementary private insurance to access faster care and better facilities.
Private insurance seekers: Higher-income individuals who prioritize private health insurance for superior service quality and shorter wait times, though they may retain public coverage.
Uninsured or underinsured: Lower-income married individuals who lack adequate health insurance coverage or rely on minimal public welfare provisions.
Uncertain navigators: People unfamiliar with Russia's complex health insurance system or unsure about their actual coverage status.
Healthy workers with minimal healthcare needs who rarely require medical treatment and thus have not experienced waiting list issues.
Regularly employed individuals with good health insurance coverage who access private or well-resourced healthcare and do not face significant waiting times.
Working people with occasional health needs who have experienced some delays in non-urgent treatments but generally manage to access care within acceptable timeframes.
Individuals with chronic conditions or ongoing healthcare needs who have encountered frustrating waiting lists for specialist appointments or procedures.
People uncertain about their healthcare experiences or those who prefer not to categorize their situation clearly, including those with unclear insurance status.
Committed atheists who reject religious belief entirely. They strongly disagree that God concerns himself with individuals, viewing this as a comforting but unfounded claim.
Secular-leaning agnostics and non-believers who are uncertain or skeptical about God's personal involvement. They tend to disagree or remain neutral on the question of divine personal concern.
Moderate believers who accept God's existence but are uncertain whether He takes personal interest in individuals. They sit in the middle, neither agreeing nor disagreeing strongly.
Practicing Christians and religious believers who affirm that God does concern Himself personally with each human being. They agree with this statement as part of their faith conviction.
Undecided individuals who find the question difficult to answer or lack strong convictions either way. They cannot choose between the options presented.

Secular environmentalists: Non-religious or skeptical of religious concepts (based on high 'No' responses to hell/heaven), they are actively engaged in environmental causes and have signed petitions about environmental issues.

Pragmatic moderates: Neither strongly religious nor strongly secular, they care about environmental issues but are less likely to take formal action like signing petitions, preferring personal lifestyle choices.
Religious but passive: Hold some religious beliefs (evident from varied heaven/hell responses), but environmental activism is not a priority for them and they have not signed environmental petitions.

Uncertain/disengaged: Show high 'Can't choose' responses across religious questions, reflecting general ambivalence about belief systems and similarly uncertain or disengaged from environmental activism.

Active believers: Strongly religious (particularly those believing in miracles), they may view environmental stewardship as a religious duty and are more likely to have signed environmental petitions.

Religious traditionalists with strong faith conviction. They believe in God's existence without doubt and feel that God is personally concerned with individual lives, viewing this as central to their worldview.
Secular skeptics who reject religious belief entirely. They disagree that God concerns Himself with human beings, seeing this as an unfounded religious claim incompatible with their non-belief.
Doubtful believers who maintain faith despite reservations. They tend toward agreement that God is personally concerned, though they hold this belief with less certainty than traditionalists.

Agnostics and spiritual pluralists who are uncertain about God's nature and personal involvement. They neither strongly agree nor disagree, viewing the question as unanswerable or dependent on one's definition of God.

Philosophical non-believers who may acknowledge a higher power but reject the concept of a personal God concerned with individuals. They disagree with the statement as too anthropomorphic and interventionist.
Secular rationalists who reject both religion and spirituality. They view themselves as non-believers who have moved away from religious frameworks entirely.
Spiritual seekers without institutional religion. They find meaning in spiritual concepts and practices outside of organized religious structures.
Traditional believers who follow a religion and integrate spirituality into their faith practice. They maintain both religious observance and spiritual conviction.
Nominal religious practitioners who follow a religion more out of cultural or family tradition than active spiritual engagement. They see religion as important but spirituality as secondary.
Uncertain or conflicted individuals who struggle to categorize themselves between secular and spiritual worldviews. They may be in transition or genuinely undecided about their beliefs.

Working-class pragmatists who see themselves as solidly middle or slightly below middle on the social ladder. They view their position as stable but not privileged, reflecting their actual economic circumstances in Russian society.

Lower-middle-class strivers who place themselves in the lower-middle range (04-06) but aspire upward. They believe their position could improve through effort and see themselves as not at the bottom despite economic pressures.
Pessimistic or realistic individuals who place themselves in the bottom third (01-03), acknowledging genuine economic hardship or social marginalization they experience in Russian society.
Upper-middle-class professionals and successful individuals who confidently place themselves in the top half (07-10), reflecting genuine advantages in income, education, or social capital.
Uncertain or disengaged respondents who struggle to self-place and may select middle positions (05-06) as a default, reflecting ambivalence about their actual social position.

Urban educated professionals with past work experience who are multilingual, having learned English in school and picked up additional languages through work or travel; they speak 2-3 languages fluently.
Rural or provincial residents with limited formal education who primarily speak their local language and basic Filipino/Tagalog; they speak one language well.
Metro Manila-based individuals with secondary education who are bilingual in English and Filipino, having acquired English through schooling; they speak two languages comfortably.

Overseas Filipino workers or their family members who have picked up additional languages through migration or international exposure, speaking 2-3 languages including English and possibly another language.

Young people from urban areas with higher education who are highly multilingual due to globalization and internet exposure, speaking three or more languages including English, Filipino, and regional languages.
Secular non-believers who actively reject religious frameworks and have no interest in scripture. They would answer 'No' as they see religious texts as irrelevant to their worldview.
Agnostics and spiritual skeptics who are indifferent to religious scripture and rarely encounter or seek it out. They would answer 'No' simply because it's not part of their life.
Culturally curious individuals with some spiritual openness who may occasionally read scripture out of intellectual interest or cultural exploration. They would answer 'Yes' but infrequently.

Believers with lingering doubts who maintain some connection to religious traditions and may read scripture occasionally for personal reflection or spiritual seeking. They would answer 'Yes' with moderate frequency.
Committed believers who actively engage with religious texts as part of their spiritual practice, despite the group's overall secular character. They would answer 'Yes' regularly.
Religious traditionalists who view abortion as morally wrong regardless of circumstances, grounded in strong religious beliefs about the sanctity of life.
Secular skeptics with little religious engagement who believe abortion in cases of financial hardship is not wrong, prioritizing practical family welfare over abstract moral rules.
Pragmatic moderates who see abortion as sometimes justifiable when families face genuine economic hardship, though they may have some moral reservations.
Conflicted believers who hold religious faith but struggle to apply it rigidly to difficult real-world situations like poverty, leaving them uncertain about this specific case.
Undecided or ambivalent respondents who lack a clear moral framework on this issue and prefer not to make a definitive judgment.

Religious traditionalists who view the Church as a moral and spiritual anchor in their lives, especially important given Venezuela's economic and social crisis. They maintain strong faith despite hardships.

Moderate believers who appreciate the Church's social work and community support but have some reservations about its institutional practices or political positions. They trust it somewhat but not completely.

Secular-minded individuals who respect the Church's charitable role but maintain emotional distance from religious institutions, viewing them as one institution among many rather than uniquely trustworthy.

Disillusioned citizens who have lost faith in most institutions including the Church, seeing it as ineffective or complicit in Venezuela's problems, or simply irrelevant to their daily survival concerns.
Pragmatic community members who value the Church primarily for its practical assistance (food programs, healthcare, education) rather than spiritual authority, trusting it as a service provider.
Progressive egalitarians who strongly reject gender discrimination in employment and believe men and women should have equal job opportunities regardless of economic conditions.
Moderate modernists who disagree with preferential treatment for men in hiring but may not feel as strongly about it, reflecting evolving views on gender equality.
Traditional conservatives who agree that men should have priority in scarce jobs, viewing this as consistent with traditional family structures and male breadwinner roles.
Pragmatic traditionalists who hold some traditional views on gender roles but are conflicted, sometimes agreeing with male job priority in economic hardship while acknowledging women's right to work.
Strong traditionalists who strongly agree that men deserve preferential access to jobs during economic scarcity, reflecting conservative Catholic values about gender roles.

Cautious self-employed professionals who have experienced or witnessed negative consequences for speaking out against government or powerful interests, making them believe public criticism of national problems carries real risks.
Confident entrepreneurs and business owners who feel secure in their social position and believe they can express opinions freely without significant personal or professional repercussions.

Politically disengaged self-employed workers who rarely engage in public discourse about national problems and therefore don't perceive direct personal risk, though they may be somewhat uncertain about the actual consequences.

Socially conscious individuals who believe in freedom of expression as a principle and feel they should be able to speak freely, though they may acknowledge that some people in Peru do face consequences.
Vulnerable informal economy workers who feel economically precarious and believe that public criticism could jeopardize their livelihoods or relationships with authorities and clients.

Disillusioned Emigrants: Those who have left Venezuela or plan to leave, viewing the country with deep pessimism due to economic collapse, political repression, and lack of opportunities. They hold very unfavorable views shaped by personal hardship and the fear of expressing dissent.

Cautious Critics: Individuals who recognize Venezuela's serious problems and hold somewhat unfavorable views, but maintain some hope for reform or gradual improvement. They are aware of the risks of speaking out but haven't completely lost faith in the country's future.

Pragmatic Acceptors: People who acknowledge Venezuela's difficulties but take a somewhat favorable view by focusing on family, community, and cultural ties that keep them rooted. They see both the country's failures and its human potential.

Institutional Loyalists: Those with strong ties to the Church and traditional institutions who maintain somewhat favorable or very favorable views despite acknowledging problems. Their trust in religious institutions influences a more hopeful national outlook.

Resilient Optimists: A small segment holding very favorable views, likely those with economic security, strong social networks, or ideological commitment to the current system. They see potential for Venezuela despite widespread criticism.

Politically disengaged pragmatists who view Venezuela unfavorably due to economic and humanitarian concerns, without strong ideological positioning. They see Venezuela's situation as a cautionary tale of state failure.

Left-leaning progressives who are critical of Venezuela's government but sympathetic to its anti-imperialist stance and original socialist goals, viewing the situation with nuance rather than blanket condemnation.
Conservative or right-leaning citizens who hold very unfavorable views of Venezuela as a failed socialist state and see it as a warning against leftist policies in Paraguay.
Younger, more socially liberal voters who focus on Venezuela's humanitarian crisis and human rights violations while remaining skeptical of both socialist and capitalist solutions.
Older, traditionally-minded citizens with strong Catholic or conservative values who view Venezuela negatively through a lens of religious and moral concerns about state atheism and social breakdown.

Pragmatic crisis responders who believe democratic institutions have failed to deliver security and economic stability, making them open to military intervention as a temporary solution to restore order.
Democratic institutionalists who have experienced or learned about the dangers of military rule in Central America and firmly reject authoritarianism regardless of circumstances.

Frustrated moderates who are deeply pessimistic about the country's trajectory but remain conflicted, seeing merit in both democratic principles and the potential efficiency of military governance during crises.
Idealistic youth who prioritize democratic values and human rights, viewing military government as inherently incompatible with progress and personal freedoms.
Disengaged skeptics who doubt either system can solve Guatemala's problems and view the question as somewhat academic given the dysfunction they perceive in both governance models.
Religious traditionalists with strong faith commitment who view the Church as a moral authority and source of spiritual guidance in their lives.
Moderate believers who respect the Church's role in society but maintain some skepticism about its institutional practices and influence.
Secular-minded citizens who are skeptical of religious institutions' power and influence, viewing the Church with little to no trust despite potential personal faith.
Socially progressive individuals who support LGBTQ+ rights and gender equality, and tend to distrust the Church's conservative positions on these issues.
Politically disengaged individuals who express low trust across all institutions including government, president, and the Church as part of broader institutional skepticism.

Secular progressives with low institutional trust. They view the Church as an outdated institution that has lost moral authority, particularly given historical scandals and the Church's conservative positions on gender and social issues.

Moderate skeptics of institutional religion. They have some residual respect for the Church's charitable work but are disappointed by its perceived hypocrisy and resistance to modern values like gender equality.

Practicing Catholics with conditional faith. They maintain personal religious belief and see value in the Church's spiritual mission, though they acknowledge institutional problems and don't blindly trust Church leadership.

Traditional believers with strong Church loyalty. They trust the Church as a moral guide and important social institution, viewing it as a stabilizing force despite acknowledging some contemporary challenges.
Indifferent or disengaged citizens. They have little opinion about the Church either way, viewing it as largely irrelevant to their daily lives in an increasingly secular urban society.

Pragmatic crisis responders who see democracy as a means to an end; if democratic institutions fail to deliver security and economic stability, they would consider military intervention as a necessary alternative to restore order.

Democratic institutionalists who have experienced or learned from Guatemala's military dictatorship history; they firmly reject military government under any circumstances, viewing democratic processes as non-negotiable despite current difficulties.

Frustrated moderates who are deeply pessimistic about the country's trajectory (aligned with the 56% seeing stagnation) and might reluctantly accept military rule if conditions deteriorate severely, though they express this ambivalently.

Socially conservative self-employed business owners who associate military government with order and property protection; they would support military intervention if they perceive threats to economic stability or security.
Ideological democrats who view military government as fundamentally illegitimate regardless of circumstances; this group is smaller but vocal in their principled opposition.

Pragmatic skeptics (urban workers and business owners): Concerned about crime and security in their communities, they tend to agree that immigrants contribute to crime problems, viewing this as a practical concern rather than ideological.

Conservative traditionalists (rural and religious communities): Holding strong views on social order and national identity, they strongly agree that immigrants increase crime, seeing this as part of broader concerns about cultural and social change.

Moderate centrists (middle-class professionals): Uncertain and divided on this issue, they may agree somewhat but lack strong conviction, reflecting ambivalence about immigration's actual effects versus stereotypes.

Progressive skeptics (younger, urban, educated individuals): Disagreeing with the statement, they view claims about immigrant crime as exaggerated or discriminatory, though this perspective is less dominant in the group.

Disengaged pragmatists (economically struggling populations): Focused on immediate economic concerns rather than immigration ideology, they may agree with crime concerns but primarily out of general anxiety about security and instability.

Institutional Trust Believers (54% trust Church highly; believe in democratic institutions and rule of law despite current difficulties). They would reject military government as a threat to democratic norms and constitutional order.

Pragmatic Crisis Responders (concerned about national problems and willing to express opinions despite risks; see immigration as beneficial). They might consider military intervention if democratic institutions fail to address crises, viewing it as a temporary solution to restore order.

Authoritarian-Leaning Skeptics (63% fear negative consequences for free speech; skeptical of immigrants; conservative on social issues). They see military government as potentially necessary to restore security and traditional order when democracy appears weak or chaotic.

Disillusioned Moderates (low trust in institutions; divided on most issues; neither strongly pro- nor anti-immigrant). They are ambivalent about military government, seeing both risks and potential benefits depending on circumstances.

Progressive Democratic Defenders (support immigrant rights and LGBTQ+ recognition; believe in democratic participation despite risks). They would firmly oppose military government as incompatible with their values of inclusion and democratic participation.

Frustrated pragmatists who see democracy as failing them. With the country at a standstill, their family struggling financially, and widespread distrust in government (65% have little or no trust), they view a military government as a potential solution to restore order and effectiveness.

Cautious democrats who fear the consequences of speaking freely (73% worry about negative consequences) and distrust institutions broadly, yet remain committed to democratic principles despite their reservations. They would not support military rule even if conditions worsen.

Economically desperate citizens whose primary concern is survival and stability for their families. Facing insufficient income and financial problems, they are willing to consider any system—including military government—if it promises economic improvement and security.

Institutional skeptics with deep religious faith who distrust government (65% have little or no trust) but maintain strong church connections (53% have a lot or some trust in the Church). They look to faith-based solutions rather than military intervention.

Principled minorities who hold progressive values (36% agree or strongly agree that same-sex couples are equally good parents) and believe in democratic resilience despite current difficulties. They firmly reject military government as incompatible with their values.

Disillusioned and pessimistic young adults who face economic uncertainty, political instability, and fear of expressing themselves freely; they are not very satisfied or not at all satisfied with their lives.
Cautiously hopeful pragmatists who acknowledge Peru's challenges but maintain some optimism about their personal futures; they are quite satisfied despite broader concerns.
Socially progressive but economically anxious youth who value democratic freedoms and LGBTQ+ rights yet struggle with life satisfaction due to limited opportunities and institutional distrust.
Politically disengaged young people who feel disconnected from institutions and are ambivalent about their life satisfaction, neither strongly satisfied nor dissatisfied.
Resilient optimists who maintain high life satisfaction despite Peru's political turmoil and institutional weakness, viewing their personal circumstances positively.

Traditional Democratic Institutionalists - Believe political parties are essential to democracy's functioning and represent the established democratic order. They see parties as necessary for organizing representation and maintaining democratic structures.

Skeptical Party Reformers - Frustrated with current political parties and institutional performance (reflected in low presidential trust), they believe democracy could function without traditional parties, perhaps through more direct or alternative mechanisms.

Pragmatic Centrists - Accept that parties exist in modern democracies but are open to the idea that alternative democratic systems could theoretically work without them, seeing it as a nuanced rather than absolute question.

Anti-Establishment Populists - Distrustful of institutional politics and party systems, they believe democracy could work better without parties, potentially through direct participation or personalist leadership.
Uncertain Pragmatists - Lack strong conviction on this abstract question and may shift views based on current political circumstances and satisfaction with democratic performance.

Disillusioned and struggling citizens who face economic hardship and political instability. They are not at all or not very satisfied with their lives due to lack of trust in institutions and limited economic opportunities.

Cautiously content working-class and middle-class Peruvians who have managed to build some stability despite challenges. They are quite satisfied with their lives, though they remain concerned about national problems and institutional trust.

Optimistic and relatively privileged individuals who feel secure in their circumstances and social position. They are very satisfied with their lives and tend to be more insulated from the broader political and economic anxieties affecting the country.

Socially conservative Catholics who prioritize traditional values and family stability as sources of life satisfaction. They find contentment in their faith and community ties, though they may worry about societal changes and moral issues.

Politically engaged and socially progressive citizens who value openness and diversity. Their life satisfaction is tempered by concern about national problems and the consequences of speaking freely about them.

Pragmatic skeptics who doubt the crime-immigration link. These young Guatemalans are influenced by their country's experience with migration and tend to see immigrants as individuals rather than a threat, viewing crime as a complex socioeconomic issue.

Cautious moderates who acknowledge some concerns about immigration and crime but don't strongly endorse the stereotype. They recognize both positive and negative aspects of immigration without taking a firm stance.

Concerned believers who agree that immigrants increase crime rates, reflecting anxieties about security and social stability. This view aligns with broader concerns about national decline evident in the group's pessimism about the country's direction.

Strong skeptics who firmly reject the notion that immigrants increase crime, viewing such claims as xenophobic. These individuals tend toward progressive values and are influenced by their country's own experience as a source of emigrants.
Disengaged or uncertain respondents who lack strong opinions on immigration and crime, reflecting the general ambivalence and standstill feeling prevalent in the group.
Progressive urbanites who embrace diversity and are skeptical of stereotypes about immigrants. They strongly disagree that immigrants increase crime, viewing such claims as xenophobic misconceptions.

Open-minded moderates who lean toward accepting diversity but have some concerns about social integration. They tend to disagree with the statement, though not strongly, seeing nuance in immigration issues.
Pragmatic centrists who are uncertain about the relationship between immigration and crime. They neither strongly agree nor disagree, viewing it as a complex empirical question without clear answers.
Tradition-conscious citizens who worry about rapid social change and perceive immigration as a potential threat to social order. They tend to agree that immigrants increase crime rates.
Strongly skeptical conservatives who believe immigration poses significant risks to public safety and cultural stability. They strongly agree that immigrants increase crime rates.

Traditional evangelical conservatives who strongly oppose same-sex adoption based on biblical teachings about family structure and traditional values. They view this as incompatible with Christian doctrine.
Conservative evangelicals with some reservations about same-sex adoption, but less absolute in their opposition. They may acknowledge practical concerns while maintaining traditional religious views.

Moderate evangelicals who distinguish between personal religious beliefs and civil rights, believing same-sex couples should have legal adoption rights even if they personally prefer traditional families.
Progressive evangelicals who actively support same-sex adoption rights, viewing it as consistent with Christian values of love and inclusion, and seeing no conflict with their faith.
Pragmatic evangelicals focused on child welfare outcomes rather than ideology, who support adoption rights for same-sex couples if evidence shows children thrive in such homes.

Traditional conservatives who prioritize defending established social norms and habits. They strongly disagree with same-sex marriage as it conflicts with their view of traditional family structures and cultural values.
Moderate traditionalists who lean toward preserving traditions but are not absolutist. They tend to disagree with same-sex marriage, though some may be conflicted or open to civil recognition.

Pragmatic moderates who value social stability but recognize changing social realities. They are divided on this issue, with some disagreeing and others agreeing, reflecting uncertainty or situational acceptance.
Progressive-leaning individuals who prefer openness to diverse traditions and habits. They agree with same-sex marriage as part of accepting social diversity and individual freedoms.
Strong progressives who actively support LGBTQ+ rights and view same-sex marriage as a fundamental equality issue. They strongly agree with same-sex marriage as essential to social justice.

Disillusioned pragmatists who have lost faith in democratic institutions. They see the government as corrupt and ineffective, and view a military government as a potential solution to restore order and progress, even if it means sacrificing democratic freedoms.

Skeptical democrats who distrust the current government but remain committed to democratic principles. They believe that despite the country's stagnation and their lack of political affiliation, abandoning democracy would only make things worse.

Economically marginalized women with minimal digital financial engagement who feel disconnected from political processes. They are ambivalent about government type, viewing both democracy and military rule as distant concepts that don't affect their daily survival.

Ideological democrats with stronger political party identification who actively reject authoritarianism. They see military government as fundamentally incompatible with their values and believe democratic reform, not replacement, is necessary.

Conditional pragmatists who would support military intervention only under extreme circumstances. They are torn between frustration with democratic dysfunction and fear of military rule, representing the most conflicted segment.
